event_model_payload.headline: Bring multimodal semantic search to the edge with EmbeddingGemma 2

Engineering teams can now safely integrate this robust tooling directly into their CI pipelines to automatically generate reliable client libraries for their own APIs, all while retaining complete licensing control over the output code.

event_model_payload.summary: How do you keep improving an AI agent after the first 80%, once it serves real production traffic and silent quality regressions return HTTP 200 OK? We are open-sourcing AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that runs beside your production agent in Google Cloud, sweeps and verifies failure clusters against conversation transcripts, and diagnoses root causes anchored to the exact deployed source snapshot.

event_model_payload.headline: Build zero-trust AI agents that judge intent, not just syntax

It highlights three primary managed defenses: Model Armor for screening edge prompts, Semantic Governance Policies for evaluating tool intent against business rules, and Agent Anomaly Detection for catching multi-turn exploits. By shifting these capabilities to the platform level, security administrators can dynamically enforce policies and neutralize complex attacks without needing to modify or redeploy the agent's underlying code.

event_model_payload.headline: Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs

Built on Google’s AI stack—including Tunix, Gemma, and Cloud TPUs—this framework eliminates manual tuning cycles, successfully demonstrating hands-off performance gains in both function calling and math reasoning models.

event_model_payload.headline: EmbeddingGemma 2: The Developer Guide
event_model_payload.summary: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-source multimodal embedding model that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Developers can use the sentence-transformers library to selectively load modular modality encoders—ranging from 270M to 740M parameters—to optimize memory usage. Additionally, Matryoshka Representation Learning enables dynamic dimension truncation down to 128d, significantly reducing vector database storage requirements while maintaining high retrieval performance.

event_model_payload.headline: Enterprise-Grade Precision for Long-Context Multimodal Embedding Inference on Cloud TPU
event_model_payload.summary: Google Cloud has natively integrated TPU support into the vLLM serving engine, allowing developers to elastically scale high-demand embedding pipelines using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). To handle massive 15K+ token contexts for models like Qwen3-Embedding-8B, the engineering team implemented TPU-specific optimizations such as hardware-safe tensor alignment, JAX/XLA compilation pre-warming, and a hybrid StepPool architecture for chunked prefill management. These enhancements achieve near-perfect numerical parity with reference GPU baselines, and developers can immediately leverage the open-sourced setup recipes on the AI-Hypercomputer GitHub to build their own high-throughput semantic retrieval applications.

event_model_payload.headline: The Anatomy of Harness Engineering: How to Evaluate, Iterate, and Guard AI Coding Agents
event_model_payload.summary: While end-to-end benchmarks like SWE-bench provide broad performance scores for AI agents, they are often expensive, slow, and lack the root-cause diagnostics needed to explain exactly where an agent's logic broke down. To solve this, developers should adopt behavioral evaluations—fast, local, unit-style tests that assert on discrete intermediate actions, such as verifying specific tool calls or file modifications rather than final string equality. By building these inexpensive micro-checks alongside macro benchmarks, engineering teams can confidently iterate on system prompts and upgrade models without the risk of regressions.

event_model_payload.headline: NailFlow AI: A Local-First Studio Assistant for Nail Artists
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Running a small nail studio means doing two jobs: the creative work clients come for, and the admin that happens between appointments. NailFlow AI is a small assistant I built for independent nail artists and beauty studios to make that second job easier.

What I Built

NailFlow turns a service inquiry into a transparent price estimate and editable client-ready copy. It can prepare a WhatsApp reply, general aftercare notes, a follow-up message, and social content such as captions, stories, hashtags, and calls to action. A local client pipeline lets the artist save a quote and track it as Draft, Follow-up, or Done. The service menu can be edited to reflect the studio's own prices and session durations.

The idea is deliberately focused: independent artists shouldn't have to rewrite the same kinds of messages all day or guess at a price on every inquiry. NailFlow gives them a draft they can review and adapt, not an automation that speaks to a client without permission.

The quote itself is calculated in code from the artist's editable menu, design complexity, and selected add-ons. AI helps with wording; it does not decide the final price. Server-side guardrails normalize detected currency amounts to the computed estimate and neutralize some common false booking-confirmation claims. These safeguards reduce risk but are not perfect, so every message should still be reviewed before sending. NailFlow does not send messages or book appointments automatically.

Demo

Live web demo: https://nail-flow-ai-lemon.vercel.app/

The deployed Vercel version demonstrates the web interface and its template fallback. It is not connected to Ollama running on my computer, so the hosted demo should not be treated as proof of live Gemma inference.

I verified the local AI path on Windows with Ollama 0.35.0 and Gemma 3 1B: the model passed a direct prompt test, and NailFlow then generated a client pack marked LOCAL AI · Generated with local Ollama inference. The hosted Vercel demo remains separate and uses its template fallback; it does not connect to the Ollama service on my PC.

Code

Public repository: https://github.com/yagnik-satani-otelier/NailFlow-AI

How I Built It

NailFlow uses a dependency-free Node.js HTTP server, vanilla JavaScript, CSS, and browser localStorage. The local-AI path is designed to use Gemma 3 1B through Ollama. The browser calls the local Node server, which forwards a structured prompt to the Ollama API on the same machine. The model can be changed with the OLLAMA_MODEL environment variable.

The prompts, validation, output parsing, deterministic pricing, and post-generation quote guardrails are visible in lib/core.js and server.js. The server sends an explicit output schema to Ollama for each generation mode to improve structured responses from a small model. When Ollama or the model is unavailable, the interface clearly labels generated content as template fallback rather than pretending it came from AI.

To run the local AI path, install Ollama, then run these commands in the repository folder:

ollama pull gemma3:1b
npm run check
npm test
npm start

Open http://127.0.0.1:4174. Generate a sample client pack and confirm that the result says LOCAL AI. I verified this path locally; if a future run says TEMPLATE MODE, that request did not use Gemma.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a solo studio, a per-message AI bill or a dependency on a hosted writing API can make a small admin assistant less practical. Local inference can avoid a NailFlow-hosted inference service or API key, while letting the studio control its own service menu, prompts, and model choice. When run with Ollama on the same machine, enquiry text goes to that local Ollama service rather than to a hosted AI provider.

There is a trade-off: the user must install and run Ollama and download a model, and a small model can produce wording that needs editing. The hosted web demo is useful for seeing the interface, while local setup is necessary to demonstrate the Gemma path. Gemma is an open-weight model; open weights should not automatically be described as OSI-approved open-source software, and model terms should be reviewed separately.

What I Tested

  • Automated suite: 20 passing unit and HTTP integration tests covering input bounds, deterministic pricing, prompt constraints, quote guardrails, parsing, template fallback, a mocked Ollama bridge, and HTTP error/security cases.
  • Browser smoke test: with mocked generation responses, I checked in-place quote and content editing, saving a quote to the client pipeline, service-duration editing, and a 390px mobile layout without horizontal overflow.
  • Real local-AI smoke test: ran ollama run gemma3:1b successfully, then generated a NailFlow client pack locally with the visible LOCAL AI label. This confirms the live inference path works on my machine; a single smoke test does not establish that every output is correct.
  • Important limitation: automated HTTP integration tests use a mock Ollama server, not the actual Gemma weights. They validate the app's bridge and guardrails but do not prove general output quality.

I haven't run a customer trial yet, so I won't claim that a nail artist has paid for or adopted the tool. A useful next validation is to put it in front of one artist, observe a sample inquiry workflow, and use their feedback to improve it.

event_model_payload.headline: People Are Vibe-Coding Clones of Every Paid App. What Actually Survives?
event_model_payload.summary:
Earlier this month, a developer in Atlanta got fed up with Adobe's cancellation fees. So he used Claude to clone the entire Adobe Creative Suite — seven apps, Photoshop through After Effects — rebuilt them from scratch in Rust, dumped them on GitHub for free, and declared "software is over."

He's not alone. Vibe-coded clones of paid apps are showing up everywhere right now: creative tools, CRMs that "drop Salesforce," all sorts of commercial software being reverse-engineered and reimplemented by individuals pointing AI agents at a problem that used to require a company.

Now, the honest part: most of these specific clones are rough. Early alpha, buggy, missing the brutal last 10% of polish that makes software actually usable. The Adobe-clone creator said so himself — "not anywhere close to ready." If you're waiting for a free Photoshop that fully replaces Photoshop, you'll be waiting a while.

But if you're only looking at whether any individual clone is good yet, you're watching the wrong thing. Something bigger just happened, and it's worth sitting with — because the wall that protected a handful of giants for twenty years just got a lot easier to climb. Let's talk about what actually survives here, and why it might be one of the better things to happen to software in a long time.

The moat was never the code. It was the cost of building it.

For decades, the giants' real protection wasn't genius. It was expense.

Building something like Photoshop, or Salesforce, or a polished premium SaaS, took armies of engineers, years of work, and tens of millions of dollars. That was the moat. Not that the software was impossible to conceive of — plenty of people knew exactly what a photo editor should do — but that actually building one at that level was out of reach for anyone without a war chest and a hiring pipeline.

That barrier is the thing that let them behave the way they did. It's why they could charge subscription rent forever, raise prices whenever, lock you into their file formats and ecosystems, make cancellation deliberately painful, and treat users as a captive audience rather than customers who could walk. Where were you going to go? Building your own was impossible. GIMP existed, and the fact that "the free alternative" was a punchline for twenty years tells you everything about how secure that moat was.

AI didn't make the clones good. Let's be clear about that. What it did was make them cheap and fast — and that's the variable that actually mattered, because cheap-and-fast is exactly the barrier the whole monopoly structure was built on. One person with an AI agent can now attempt, in weeks, what used to need a funded team and years. The clone doesn't have to be finished to matter. The wall just has to become climbable, and it did.

What actually survives (because it isn't the clones)

Let me be straight, because it's the honest center of this: most of these clones will die. They'll stall in alpha, or the maintainer will lose interest, or they'll never close the last-10% gap that separates "impressive demo" from "thing I trust with my work." Free clone graveyards are a real thing, and AI makes it easier to start a project, not to finish and maintain one.

So the clones themselves, mostly, won't survive. Here's what does, permanently:

The giants can no longer assume they're the only option. For twenty years, "build your own" was not a sentence anyone finished. Now it is — credibly, cheaply, repeatedly. And you don't actually need the clone to be perfect for this to change everything. You need it to be possible. A monopoly's power comes from the absence of alternatives; the moment a credible alternative becomes cheap to mount, the monopoly has to start behaving like it has competition, whether or not any single competitor wins. Possibility is the product here, not polish.

That shift doesn't expire when the clones do. The cost wall fell, and it is not going back up.

Why this is genuinely good — and not just satisfying to say

It would be easy to make this purely about schadenfreude. I want to make the real argument instead, because it's stronger: this is good for reasons that have nothing to do with anyone's feelings about Big Tech.

Monopoly pricing dies when "build your own" becomes thinkable. You don't even need people to actually build the alternative — you need the giants to know they could. That alone caps what they can charge and how badly they can treat you, because the escape hatch is finally real. Prices, terms, and lock-in all have to get more honest when the door isn't locked anymore. Users win, directly.

Leverage returns to the small side for the first time in a generation. For two decades the relationship was entirely one-directional: accept the subscription, accept the price hike, tolerate the slow enshittification, or leave — to nothing. There was no "or else." Now there's a credible "or else," and leverage you can't negotiate from is the whole game. That's new, and it's healthy.

Innovation decentralizes. When building serious software required armies, only the well-funded could do it, which meant software got built to serve shareholders and quarterly targets. When it requires one motivated person and an AI, a thousand people can try — and some of them will build things the giants never would have, because they're scratching their own itch instead of optimizing a funnel. Not all of it will be good. But it'll be varied, and variety is where the genuinely new things come from.

And the companies most exposed are the ones who earned it. Notice why that developer built the Adobe clones: cancellation fees. Resentment. The feeling of being squeezed. The giants most vulnerable to this are precisely the ones who leaned hardest on their moat — aggressive pricing, hostile lock-in, treating loyal users like a billing relationship. The companies that actually treated people well have the least to fear. That's not revenge. That's the market finally doing the thing it's supposed to do.

The part that's hard to say politely

There's an irony here that's worth naming plainly, because it's real and it matters.

The giants pushed AI harder than anyone. They built it, embedded it in everything, sold it as the inevitable future — and, crucially, many of them cited AI-driven efficiency while laying off thousands of their own engineers. The message to workers was unmistakable: AI makes your expertise cheap, which makes you replaceable.

And now that same AI is making their moats cheap. The barrier that made them untouchable — the sheer cost of building software this good — is the exact thing AI is dissolving. The tool they wielded to cut their labor costs is the tool eroding the walls that let them charge rent.

This isn't childish "haha, suffer." It's something more structural, and harder to argue with: you cannot spend years telling the entire world that AI makes expertise cheap and replaceable, and then act shocked when AI makes your expertise — your product, your moat, your pricing power — cheap and replaceable too. The disruption they aimed at their own workforce turned around and pointed back at them. If you live by the AI-efficiency argument, you don't get to be surprised when you're disrupted by it. The symmetry is just honest.

The role AI is actually playing here

Strip away the drama and AI's specific role in all this is clear: it's the great equalizer.

It collapsed the one variable — build cost — that was holding the entire monopoly structure upright. For the first time, the ability to build serious, ambitious software isn't gated behind a company's balance sheet. It's in the hands of individuals. That's a genuine redistribution of a capability that was concentrated for decades, and it happened fast.

Now, the honest double-edge: the same AI that lets a solo dev clone Adobe also helps Adobe defend itself. The giants have more compute, more data, more distribution, more lawyers. AI arms both sides. But — and this is the whole point — it arms the small side far more, in relative terms, because the giants were already powerful and the little guy had essentially nothing. Handing a new weapon to someone who already has an army changes little; handing the same weapon to someone who had a stick changes everything. The uplift is asymmetric, and it favors the underdog. That asymmetry is why this is disruptive instead of just incremental.

Let's not kid ourselves, though

If I only told you the optimistic half, you'd be right not to trust me, so here's the honest counterweight.

The legal fights are coming, and they'll be ugly. "Clean-room reimplementation" — functional replication without copying code — is a real and defensible concept, but trade dress, trademarks, and the exact line between "inspired by" and "copy of" are not settled, and the giants have the lawyers to make that line expensive to approach. Some of these clones will get sued into oblivion regardless of their technical merits.

And "free clone" is not automatically a win for anyone. Software nobody maintains becomes a security liability. A clone without support, updates, and a community is a trap you walk into the day its single maintainer gets bored. The open-source graveyard is full of "free alternatives" that were genuinely better for about eight months. AI lowered the cost of starting; it did almost nothing for the cost of sustaining, which is where most of these die.

None of that undoes the core shift. But anyone selling you "software is free now, the giants are finished" is selling you the same overconfidence from the other direction. The wall fell. The giants will adapt, litigate, and survive. It's the uncontested part of their power that's gone.

What actually survives

So, back to the question in the title. What survives this wave of clones?

Not most of the clones. They'll do what early, unmaintained, one-person software usually does.

What survives is the end of an era — the one where a handful of companies could build an unbreakable wall out of engineering cost, sit behind it charging rent forever, and treat both users and workers as disposable, because there was genuinely nowhere else to go. AI knocked a hole in that wall. The giants aren't finished; they'll adapt and they'll endure. But they will never again have the uncontested dominance they had, because "build your own" stopped being impossible, and a threat that's cheap to mount is a threat that never fully goes away.

And for an industry that spent the last few years telling its own people they were replaceable by AI, there's a fitting symmetry in watching that same AI make monopoly itself a little more replaceable too.

That's not the end of software. It's a shift in who gets to make it — away from the few with the war chests, toward the many with an idea and an AI agent. Most of them will fail. That's fine. The point was never that everyone wins. The point is that, for the first time in a long time, the giants can lose. And a world where the giants can lose is a healthier one than the one we had.

Honest questions, and I want the real answers, not the comfortable ones: is AI collapsing the cost of cloning software actually good — the end of monopoly rent and lock-in — or does it just leave us a graveyard of abandoned clones and a decade of lawsuits? And the uncomfortable one: after years of "AI will replace you" pointed at engineers, is there genuine justice in AI coming for the giants' moats — or does it just feel good to say? I genuinely go back and forth.

Context & sources: this piece is anchored in the early-October 2026 release of ArtCraft — Atlanta developer Brandon Thomas's suite of seven open-source, AI-assisted "clean-room" reimplementations of Adobe's creative apps (Photocraft, Vectorcraft, Filmcraft, Lightcraft, Printcraft, Effectcraft, Designcraft), built with Claude Opus 5.5 in Rust and widely covered (Gizmodo, PetaPixel, KDnuggets, Phoronix, and others). The creator has described the apps as early alpha and "not anywhere close to ready." The broader "SaaSpocalypse" framing — the idea that AI-collapsed build costs threaten subscription software — and related clone projects (REA and others) are drawn from the same October 2026 reporting. Specifics are current-as-of-writing and moving fast; treat the trend as the story rather than any single clone's readiness.

event_model_payload.headline: 48-Hour Field Notes: I Stopped Treating the Reply as the Run
event_model_payload.summary:
I opened a fresh notebook because a polished reply kept arriving before any process on my side had started. The text looked complete, named a command, and even described a passing check that I had not executed. Why was I ready to copy that sentence into the log as if it were an observation? A chat transcript is not a process table, and it cannot show which binary actually ran.

That gap is the whole job for these notes, not a product tour and not a scoreboard. I wanted one place to ask a model for a patch, and another place to run a narrow command where I could read the exit myself. If those two records disagree, which one deserves the green mark in my notes? I wrote the rule down before I asked for another suggestion, because a fluent paragraph can impersonate a result.

What I tried in the first twelve hours

I started by splitting the work into two witnesses that are not allowed to grade each other. The first witness is a free model session, useful when I want a draft command or a short explanation without opening a paid console. The second witness is a free server session, useful when I need a shell that is not my laptop and not the model's imagination. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I am using those two availability claims only, and I am not treating a marketing page as a measured lab.

I did not record a model name, a quota, a machine size, or a promise that the free option will still look the same next month. Those details change, and inventing them would make these notes lie with a straight face. What I can repeat is the order of operations, which is dull on purpose and hard to fake. Ask, capture, hash the text, run an allowlisted command, then write the exit code beside the hash.

Here is the question I kept asking whenever the reply sounded finished. Did any process outside the chat actually start, and did it finish with a code I can quote? If I cannot answer that, the suggestion stays in a draft folder, even when the wording is clean. A free server is not magic here, because a free shell can still be the wrong tree, the wrong user, or a job that never left the queue.

The notebook I would actually rerun

The artifact below is a small recorder, not a benchmark and not a claim that I timed a vendor. I labeled the sample paths as examples, and I would run them on whatever host I was given rather than trust a pasted success story. You can drop the file on the server, point it at an allowlist, and refuse to print a green line unless the command exits zero. Would I merge a patch because the model said this script already passed? No, I would not, and the script is written to make that laziness slightly harder.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Suggestion ledger. Example workflow, not a recorded benchmark."""

import hashlib
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ALLOW = {
    "py_compile": [sys.executable, "-m", "py_compile"],
    "unit_check": [sys.executable, "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests", "-q"],
}

def stamp(label, text):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    return {
        "label": label,
        "sha256": digest,
        "chars": len(text),
        "at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

def run_allowed(key, extra):
    if key not in ALLOW:
        raise SystemExit(f"refusing unknown job: {key}")
    cmd = ALLOW[key] + list(extra)
    proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=120)
    return {
        "cmd": cmd,
        "code": proc.returncode,
        "stdout_sha256": hashlib.sha256(proc.stdout.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "stderr_sha256": hashlib.sha256(proc.stderr.encode()).hexdigest(),
    }

def main():
    suggestion = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    job = sys.argv[2]
    record = {
        "suggestion": stamp("model_reply", suggestion),
        "run": run_allowed(job, sys.argv[3:]),
    }
    record["agree"] = record["run"]["code"] == 0
    print(json.dumps(record, indent=2))
    return 0 if record["agree"] else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

The commands I actually want in the notes are boring, and that is a feature rather than a lack of ambition. I save the raw reply first, then I compile, then I decide whether a unit discovery is even on the allowlist for this host. A model can propose a piped install, and this recorder will not grow a new key just because the paragraph sounded urgent. Why give a draft the right to invent its own shell history?

mkdir -p notes/day1
# Save the raw completion yourself. Do not let the model write this file.
cp reply.txt notes/day1/reply.txt
python3 ledger.py notes/day1/reply.txt py_compile path/to/changed_module.py
echo "ledger_exit=$?"

I also keep a second command for the case where the server and my laptop do not share a tree. I print the host, the user, and the executable before I trust a zero, because a green code on the wrong machine is just a different story. This check is about identity of the run, not a feeling about how fast the free box answered.

python3 - <<'PY'
import getpass, platform, sys
print(platform.node(), getpass.getuser(), sys.executable)
PY
# Sketch only: replace the alias with the host your panel actually shows.
ssh free-host 'python3 -m py_compile path/to/changed_module.py; echo exit:$?'

I should label that ssh line as a sketch. The host alias free-host is a placeholder, not a hostname I measured, and your free server panel may name the box differently. If the panel does not give you a shell, this branch of the notes simply stops. A free model can still draft the patch, but it cannot substitute for the missing exit code.

What broke when I let the reply grade itself

The first break was social, not technical, and it showed up as soon as the paragraph said the check already passed. I had not started the server job, yet my fingers wanted to write verified next to the suggestion hash. Who was I trying to impress with that word, the future reader or my own impatience? I deleted the word and left the hash alone until ledger_exit existed.

The second break was a mismatched command that still looked related enough to fool a tired note. The reply described unittest, while the only allowlisted job I was willing to run that hour was py_compile, so a clean compile was not the test the paragraph had claimed. A zero from the compiler does not prove the tests, and a model's summary does not prove the compiler ran. I started writing the job key in the same line as the claim, so a later reader can see the gap without guessing.

The third break was environmental, and it is the one I would repeat the warning for. A free server can boot with a different working directory, a different user, or a queue that never dispatched the command I thought I had sent. If the ledger file is missing, I do not infer success from silence, because silence is how a dropped job disguises itself. Did the process start, and did it finish, or did I only receive a sentence about finishing?

A decision table I can reuse tomorrow

I do not want a score that pretends to measure model quality, because I never built that experiment and I will not fake the rows. This table only decides whether my notes may say ran, or must say draft. The columns are evidence I can point at, not feelings about how confident the wording sounded.

What I hold Reply only Server log only Both, and codes match the claim
Note status draft incomplete candidate
May I say verified? no no only for that job key
Next action save hash, do not patch rerun or fix the host read the diff, then decide
Failure I expect fluent false pass wrong tree or no dispatch still review the diff

A candidate is not a merge. It means the command I allowlisted exited in a way that matches the narrow claim, on a host I can name in the note. If the reply promised tests and I only compiled, the row stays incomplete even when the compiler was happy. Would I widen the allowlist mid-session because the model asked nicely? No, that change belongs in a separate note, after I have read the new command.

What I would repeat, and what I would not

I would repeat the capture step, the allowlist, and the refusal to write verified without ledger_exit in the same folder. I would also repeat the host line, because a free server is only useful if I can tell it apart from my laptop and from the chat. The free model access is the part I would keep for drafting, especially when I want another wording of a failing traceback before I open a paid seat. The free server option is the part I would keep for the run, because a suggestion that never meets a shell is still just a suggestion.

I would not repeat any sentence that quotes a quota, a GPU name, or a latency number I did not measure on that day. I would not pipe a model command into a shell, and I would not let the recorder accept arbitrary arguments from the reply text. I would not use this notebook to judge which vendor is best, because two availability switches are not a leaderboard. If your work needs a private dataset, a signed production host, or a change window with an on-call owner, do not rehearse that change on a free shared server just because the reply looked ready.

People who should skip this approach are easy to name, and I would rather name them than pretend the ledger fits every team. Skip it if you cannot read the server log yourself, or if policy forbids sending even a redacted traceback to an outside model. Skip it if the patch touches credentials, production data, or a service you cannot roll back before the next coffee. Skip it if you need a compliance attestation, because a field notebook is not an audit, and a free tier is not a contract I am willing to invent.

Limits I am leaving in the note

This workflow does not prove that the model understood the code, and it does not prove that the server matches production. A timeout of 120 seconds in the example is a guard for the sketch, not a service level I negotiated with anyone. py_compile catches syntax, not behavior, and unittest discover only helps if those tests already exist and already mean something. The hashes tell me whether the text changed, not whether the text was wise.

I also cannot tell you that the free model list or the free server button will remain in the same place, with the same limits, next week. Check the console you actually have, and write down what you see instead of copying these notes as if they were a status page. If the free server never gives you a shell, stop at the draft and run the allowlisted command somewhere you do control. A missing witness is a result, and it should look like a missing witness in the file.

If you already use MonkeyCode, the useful part is ordinary: open the free model path when you need a draft, open the free server path when you need a shell, and keep their outputs in separate files. I would still read the diff myself before I land anything, because agreement on an exit code is not agreement that the change is the one I wanted. The notebook is there so my future self can see what ran, what never started, and what I refused to call done.

event_model_payload.headline: Self-hosted SaaS boilerplate: what \"self-hosted\" has to mean, and a checklist
event_model_payload.summary:
"Self-hosted" has become a checkbox on boilerplate landing pages, and the
checkbox is usually true in the narrowest sense: yes, the Node process can
run on your VPS. Then you read the .env.example and find the auth
provider's API key, the managed database URL, the queue service token, the
email API key and the file-storage bucket. The process is yours; the
product is theirs. This article proposes a definition strict enough to be
useful, and turns it into questions you can ask any kit — including ours.

A definition

A SaaS foundation is self-hosted when the product keeps working, for all
its users, with nothing but the servers you operate and the one payment
processor you cannot avoid. Everything else is optional or replaceable
with something you run:

  • Sign-in works with your database alone. External identity providers are a feature you add, not a dependency you start with.
  • Email goes out through any SMTP server, including your own; a hosted email API is a configuration, not a requirement.
  • Background jobs run inside the application, backed by your database, and survive a restart.
  • Files go to a local directory or to any S3-compatible service you choose, including one you run.
  • Analytics, error reporting and monitoring are opt-in and can point at self-hosted tools.
  • The payment processor is the exception, and its failure mode is bounded: with no key configured, the application runs, and billing is simply off.

By that definition most "self-hostable" kits are not. That is not an
accusation; it is a consequence of building on a BaaS. It is worth knowing
before you sign a data-processing agreement that lists sub-processors you
did not choose.

Why it matters, concretely

The bill. A rented stack is five invoices with five floors. A binary on
a server is the server. We priced it in
The rented stack.

The questionnaire. The first enterprise customer sends a security
questionnaire. "Where is the data, who are the sub-processors, how do you
delete a user?" With a self-hosted foundation the answers are one country,
three names and a button. See Keeping a SaaS in the EU
for what self-hosting settles and what it does not.

The exit. When a vendor changes pricing or terms, a self-hosted product
moves by copying a binary and a database dump. A product built on managed
auth moves by re-implementing auth.

The checklist

Ask these of any kit. The honest answers are usually in the .env.example.

  1. Delete every third-party key from the configuration. Does it boot, can a user sign up, sign in, reset a password? If sign-in needs an external provider to exist, it is not self-hosted.
  2. Which database, and can I run it myself? PostgreSQL on your server counts. A vendor's "serverless Postgres" with a connection string does not, unless the kit also runs against a plain instance.
  3. Where do background jobs run? In-process with a database table: yes. A hosted queue with a token: no.
  4. How does email leave? SMTP to any host: yes. Only through one API vendor: no.
  5. Where do uploads go? Local disk or any S3-compatible endpoint: yes. One vendor's bucket API: no.
  6. What happens with no payment key? The app should run and hide billing. A crash, or a checkout button that errors, means the unconfigured path was never tested.
  7. What runs in production? One process you can list is better than a platform-specific build output. Count the runtimes: Node, PHP, Redis, workers.
  8. Can I read all of it? Lines of code you will own, not features advertised. If the answer is "it's a monorepo, you don't need to read the packages", you are renting with extra steps.
  9. Is the licence perpetual, and does it cover client work?
  10. Does the repository come with a way to run everything locally, including the external pieces (identity provider, S3, mail, payment sandbox)? If the vendor's own demo needs their cloud, so will yours.

How GoVueKit answers

  1. Boots and signs users up with a database file and nothing else: argon2id passwords, verification, reset, magic links, TOTP, session revocation. Google, GitHub, Microsoft and any OIDC provider are switched on by adding keys; the unconfigured path is tested in CI.
  2. PostgreSQL and SQLite, same migrations, same generated queries, both engines in the test matrix. DB_DRIVER decides.
  3. Jobs are rows in your database, run in-process, retried, surviving redeploys.
  4. SMTP by default; Resend is an option behind the same Mailer interface.
  5. STORAGE=disk or STORAGE=s3 against any endpoint (the labs uses MinIO).
  6. No Stripe key means billing is off and the app is otherwise complete; the tests cover that configuration because it is the one most deployments run.
  7. One static binary, ~27 MB, the Vue app embedded. Traefik for TLS if you want automatic certificates. Nothing else.
  8. About 11 000 lines of Go, 19 packages, one migration file, and a DECISIONS.md that explains the non-obvious choices — public before you buy, at github.com/kOlapsis/govuekit.
  9. €199 once, perpetual, lifetime updates of the major version, unlimited end products including client work.
  10. One compose file, no account: 
curl -fsSLO https://govuekit.dev/labs/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d   # app + PostgreSQL + Dex (OIDC) + MinIO (S3) + stripe-mock + Mailpit

The tenth question is the one to start with. A kit that can boot its whole
world on your laptop can boot it on your server; one that cannot has
already told you where it really lives.

Originally published on govuekit.dev. GoVueKit is a complete Go + Vue 3 SaaS codebase you buy once and own; the whole stack runs on your machine with one docker compose up: https://govuekit.dev/labs

event_model_payload.headline: Recover a delayed verification callback
event_model_payload.summary:
Recover a delayed callback without creating duplicate sessions. The runnable local example stores state in SQLite, enforces a deadline and rejects late permission grants. Its callback channel is explicitly synthetic: it is not a live signature verifier.

What you will build

Recover a delayed callback without creating duplicate sessions. The runnable local example stores state in SQLite, enforces a deadline and rejects late permission grants. Its callback channel is explicitly synthetic: it is not a live signature verifier.

Run and inspect the three outcomes 

for scenario in success reject unavailable; do
  curl -fsS https://gridzen.ai/console/api/quickstart/trial \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"task":"identity_onboarding","scenario":"'"$scenario"'"}'
done

Expected output (synthetic) 

{
  "mode": "synthetic_fixture",
  "source": "local_response_trial",
  "task": "identity_onboarding",
  "scenario": "success",
  "verified": false,
  "real_person_verified": false,
  "billable": false,
  "amount_minor": 0,
  "upstream_calls": 0,
  "result": {
    "status": "Approved",
    "reason": "synthetic_scenario",
    "hosted_url": null
  },
  "business_decision": "caller_owned",
  "next_step": "connect_verified_account_for_persisted_sandbox",
  "production_available_from_this_trial": false
}

Local state machine: restart, duplicates and deadlines

The local script uses only fixture identifiers. Run the code and tests in the linked repository; no account or provider key is required. Production callbacks need their own authorized signature verifier.

git clone https://github.com/immurray/gridzen-developer-kit.git
cd gridzen-developer-kit
python3 examples/verification_delivery/delivery.py identity --db /tmp/gridzen-local-delivery.sqlite3
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install pytest
.venv/bin/python -m pytest examples/verification_delivery/test_delivery.py -q

Decide what your app does next

Treat success as a fixture branch, not real-person approval. For reject, show a recoverable message or review path. For unavailable, leave the outcome unknown and avoid silently granting permission. In a real integration, bind tenant, account and session; verify the provider notification, re-read authoritative state and apply your business policy before changing permissions.

Limits and production handoff

No documents, phone numbers, credentials or real users are accepted by this trial. Production is a separate owner-approved free pilot. Current phone production provides basic validity only; hosted identity requires current confirmed free allowance and applicable supplier rights. Real payments remain disabled.

Synthetic integration example; no real person verified, no OTP, no production permission and no payment.

Run without signup · Get task guidance · Source and tests

event_model_payload.headline: RagLeap Core v0.10.1 — I shipped 2 releases in 44 mins after Windows broke everything
event_model_payload.summary:
I shipped ragleap-core v0.10.0 with login throttling, Setup tab, and a read-only skill for coding agents. 44 minutes later I shipped v0.10.1.

Why? First real Windows test with Docker Desktop.

A local PostgreSQL was already on port 5433. Installer stopped. That's it.

That's the most honest bug report you'll get in AI.

What shipped in v0.10.0 (hardening):

  • Login throttling: 10 bad API keys in 5 mins → 15 min 429 lock with Retry-After. Proxy-aware via TRUSTED_PROXIES, off with AUTH_THROTTLE=off
  • Setup tab + GET /setup/status: Shows what's configured/missing, never shows secrets, zero AI calls
  • Read-only skill for coding agents: manifest + small client (health, employees, ask). Can't change anything by design
  • Ollama context 8192 default: Long docs no longer silently cut
  • Installer checks: Free disk check (4GB / 14GB for local AI), refuses if Compose project name already used, can use Ollama app already running on Win/Mac. Added install.ps1 PowerShell installer
  • Security: Every third-party GitHub Action pinned to exact commit

**

What shipped in v0.10.1 (Windows reality):

**

This is where it gets real.

  • Free host ports: All ports are now settings — APP_PORT 8000, DB_PORT 5433, VOICE_PORT 8766, NEO4J 7475/7688, REDIS 6380. On fresh install, installer picks next free port if busy, writes to .env, uses it for dashboard link. Existing .env never changed.
  • ragleap key --rotate: Writes new random API key to .env, restarts only app, checks old key is refused + new accepted, prints new link. DB untouched.
  • Browser instead of printed key: On desktop (Win/Mac/Linux with display, no SSH), opens dashboard in browser, no key in terminal. Servers/SSH/CI still print link. RAGLEAP_NO_BROWSER=1 to always print.
  • Fixed: DB exists check matched ANY Docker volume with same name, even unrelated installs → now matches only this setup's volume. API docs now says needs x-api-key header (401 by design).

Honest limits (we list these in release notes):

  • Tested on one Windows machine with Docker Desktop, Gemini/Ollama/skip menu set to skip. Ollama on Windows not tested yet
  • One-liner irm ... | iex fails on that machine, cause unknown. Use two-step: $s = irm ; iex $s
  • PATH hint writes for bash, not PowerShell
  • Windows reserved excluded ranges not detected by busy-port check
  • While browser launches, key briefly visible in process list

**

What is RagLeap Core?

**

Self-hosted AI Business OS — 46 autonomous AI Employees (9 core + 37 vertical like Recruiter, Real Estate Agent, Legal Intake), Graph RAG (Neo4j), multi-channel (WhatsApp/Telegram/Discord/Voice), BYOK 19 providers + Ollama local, MIT licensed.

or Windows

$s = irm https://ragleap.com/install.ps1; iex $s

18 stars → aiming 20⭐️
