event_model_payload.headline: Best Enterprise AI Gateways
event_model_payload.summary:
TL;DR

  • An enterprise AI gateway sits between your applications (and, increasingly, your agents and employees) and every model provider. It handles routing, failover, budgets, access control, guardrails and audit logs in one place, so you stop rebuilding them in every codebase.
  • Judge an enterprise AI gateway on five things: overhead under real load, governance depth, where it can be deployed, MCP support, and how much of your actual AI traffic it can see.
  • This guide compares the five leading enterprise AI gateways: Bifrost, Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management, Portkey and LiteLLM.
  • Bifrost is the strongest all-round enterprise AI gateway for teams that want a dedicated, self-hostable gateway with MCP governance and, through Bifrost Edge, coverage of AI tools running on employee laptops. The other four each win in a narrower situation, covered below.
  • Two things changed this year and belong in any procurement conversation: Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, and LiteLLM had a PyPI supply chain incident in March.

A couple of years ago, a gateway conversation meant one thing: stop pasting provider keys into config files and get a single invoice. That's still part of the job. But platform teams now get harder questions. Which MCP servers can our agents reach? Who approved them? Why did one team's spend triple in a week? And what is the sales team pasting into the desktop chat app nobody configured?

An enterprise AI gateway is where those answers live, or at least where they should live. The catch is that the category has stretched. Some products are purpose-built LLM gateways, some are classic API gateways with AI policies added on top, and one just got bought by a security vendor. Picking between them on a feature checklist gets you a spreadsheet full of green ticks and no real answer.

Disclosure: Bifrost is built by Maxim AI, which also publishes this blog. Weigh the ranking with that in mind. Each section below says plainly where the alternatives are the better call.

What an enterprise AI gateway actually does

At its core, an AI gateway is a reverse proxy for model traffic. Your apps talk to one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway translates, routes and retries across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

What turns an AI gateway into an enterprise AI gateway is everything around that proxy: identity (SSO and roles), budgets per team or customer, audit trails you can hand to a compliance officer, deployment inside your own network, and policy that applies the same way whether the caller is a service, an autonomous agent or a person. If you want the longer version of that argument, the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide walks through the capability matrix in detail.

What to check before you shortlist an enterprise AI gateway

  • Overhead under load. Every request passes through the gateway, so its processing time is added to every model call. It's invisible on a single chat completion and very visible when an agent chains forty calls.
  • Governance depth. Per-team budgets, rate limits, role-based access and audit logs should be enforced at the infrastructure layer, not left to each app team's good intentions.
  • Where it runs. Regulated teams often need in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment. A gateway that only exists as a hosted service is a non-starter for them.
  • MCP. If agents call tools, the gateway needs to control which servers and tools they can reach, and with whose credentials.
  • Guardrails. PII redaction, secrets detection and prompt injection checks need to run before data reaches a model, with a clear choice between block, redact and log.
  • Coverage. A gateway only governs traffic that reaches it. Ask what happens to the AI tools people install themselves.

Enterprise AI gateways at a glance

If you only have a minute, this is the table to read. Bifrost is the go-to enterprise AI gateway because it covers model calls, MCP tool calls and agent traffic in one gateway, runs entirely inside your own infrastructure, and is the only one here that also reaches the AI tools running on employee laptops, through Bifrost Edge.

Capability Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
Form factor Standalone gateway in Go, single binary Plugins on Kong Gateway or Konnect Policies on Azure API Management Gateway plus hosted platform Python SDK and proxy
Model coverage 10,000+ models, 25+ providers Major hosted and self-hosted providers Azure OpenAI plus other registered backends 1,600+ models 100+ providers
Failover and balancing Weighted routing, retries, fallbacks, adaptive balancing and circuit breakers (Enterprise) Load balancing and semantic routing Backend load balancing Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Routing and fallbacks
Semantic caching Yes (Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) Yes (plugin) Yes (policies with Redis) Select Enterprise plans Yes (Qdrant, Valkey, Redis)
MCP governance Native MCP gateway, tool filtering, per-user OAuth, Code Mode (up to 92.8% fewer input tokens) AI MCP Proxy and OAuth2 plugins MCP servers inside API Management MCP Gateway MCP gateway
Guardrails Content safety, PII and secrets detection, plus AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and more (Enterprise) Prompt guard plugins Content safety policy Built-in guardrails with PII detection Integrations, some need a license
AI on laptops (desktop, browser, coding agents) Yes, with Bifrost Edge Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only
Our verdict Best all-round enterprise choice Best if Kong already runs your APIs Best for Azure-only estates Best managed option, especially for Palo Alto shops Best for Python-first teams

The sections below take each gateway in turn, starting with the one we'd pick.

1. Bifrost

Bifrost is an open-source (Apache 2.0) enterprise AI gateway written in Go. It gives you one OpenAI-compatible interface to 10,000+ models across 25+ providers, and the drop-in setup means moving an existing app over is a single base URL change. It ships as one binary, so it runs on a VM, Kubernetes, private cloud or a fully disconnected network, and most teams are live the same day.

Speed is the headline. Bifrost's published benchmarks show about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In the head-to-head run on AWS EC2 (500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), Bifrost sustained 424 requests per second against 44.84 for LiteLLM, with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds versus 90.72 seconds.

On the governance side, virtual keys carry budgets and rate limits that can be set per key, team, customer or model. In the Enterprise tier, governance runs off the identity provider you already use (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider), with SCIM 2.0 directory sync, fine-grained RBAC and data access control, and reusable access profiles so platform teams set the rules once. Routing combines weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks to another provider, and semantic caching serves stored answers to similar prompts, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2024540241844224013-667'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2024540241844224013&theme=dark" }

The MCP gateway is where it pulls ahead of most of this list. It governs which MCP servers and tools agents can use, with filtering at the client, request and virtual key level, and per-user OAuth so each person connects under their own account. Its Code Mode has the model write a short script to orchestrate tools instead of loading every tool definition into context, which cuts input token use by up to 92.8% across large tool sets. In a 508-tool run, Code Mode took the cost from $377 to $29 with a 100% task pass rate. The full numbers are in the MCP gateway cost and access control write-up.

Then there's Bifrost Edge, which the other gateways here simply don't have an answer for. Edge runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser AI, terminal coding agents and the MCP servers they connect to through your Bifrost gateway, after a one-time SSO sign-in. Only AI traffic is routed, and nothing else on the device is inspected. The same virtual keys, budgets and guardrails apply to tools nobody wired up on purpose, with content safety, PII and secrets detection on requests and responses, plus connections to AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR, Check Point Guard and others. Admins can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally, and a denial is enforced on the device, not just flagged in a dashboard. Rollout goes through the device management you already run: Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud.

For regulated teams, the enterprise tier adds clustering (a peer-to-peer cluster with no leader, so an outage one node sees is acted on by all of them), adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs that can't be altered, secret management through AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment where no prompts or responses leave your infrastructure. Bifrost is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR compliant, and multiple Fortune 500 companies run it in production across financial services, healthcare, technology, pharmaceuticals and defense.

Where to be careful: the enterprise depth (identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail integrations, vault integrations and in-VPC deployment) sits in the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint, so budget for it separately, and it's still offered through early access, so pilot it on a subset of devices before a fleet-wide push.

Best for: Bifrost is built for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require best-in-class performance, scalability, and reliability. It serves as a centralized AI gateway to route, govern, and secure all AI traffic across models and environments with ultra low latency. Bifrost unifies LLM gateway, MCP gateway, and Agents gateway capabilities into a single platform.

Designed for regulated industries and strict enterprise requirements, it supports air-gapped deployments, VPC isolation, and on-prem infrastructure. It provides full control over data, access, and execution, along with robust security, policy enforcement, and governance capabilities.

2. Kong AI Gateway

Kong AI Gateway is what happens when a mature API gateway learns about LLMs. If Kong already fronts your APIs, the pitch writes itself: same control plane, same plugin model, same team on call. The AI layer adds provider routing, token-based rate limiting, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models.

MCP arrived with Gateway 3.12 in October 2025. The AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose existing REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server, with ACLs applied to both tool discovery and tool invocation, and a companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic.

The trade-offs are practical ones. Kong's docs list the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and the OAuth2 plugin was still labelled tech preview there at the time of writing. And if Kong isn't already in your stack, standing up a full API gateway platform just for LLM traffic is a lot of machinery for the job.

Best for: organizations already standardized on Kong that want AI traffic on the control plane they already run.

3. Azure API Management

For Azure-first companies this is the path of least resistance. Microsoft's AI gateway capabilities aren't a separate product, they're a set of policies on top of API Management. A token limit policy enforces per-consumer quotas (and can count prompt tokens up front so oversized requests never reach the backend), a metrics policy sends token usage to Application Insights, and semantic caching runs on Azure Managed Redis or another RediSearch-compatible cache. LLM backends can be load balanced, and Entra ID handles authentication.

MCP support is real too. You can expose APIs as MCP servers and, per the June 2026 release notes, package them into products to control who gets what.

The costs are portability and tier. Capabilities vary by API Management service tier, everything is configured through policy XML, and the whole design assumes you live in Azure. Multi-cloud or on-prem estates will feel the friction.

Best for: Azure-centric enterprises with an existing API Management investment and security teams that already trust Entra and Azure Monitor.

4. Portkey (now Prisma AIRS AI Gateway)

Portkey made its name as the developer-friendly managed gateway: one API for 1,600+ models, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails with PII detection, budgets, RBAC and detailed logs. It added an MCP Gateway in January 2026, the core gateway is open source, and deployment options run from SaaS to private cloud, VPC and fully self-hosted. Enterprise plans bring SAML 2.0 SSO and audit logs.

The big news is ownership. Palo Alto Networks announced it would acquire Portkey and closed the deal on May 29, 2026, and the product now appears as the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. For existing Palo Alto customers that's a neat consolidation, with the gateway sitting next to runtime security and identity tooling. For everyone else it's a fair moment to ask about roadmap and packaging, even though Palo Alto said existing and new Portkey customers will continue to be supported. One more detail: per Portkey's caching docs, semantic caching is limited to select Enterprise plans.

Best for: teams that want a managed, quick-to-adopt gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem.

5. LiteLLM

LiteLLM is where a lot of teams start, for good reason. It's an MIT-licensed Python SDK plus a self-hosted proxy with 100+ providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing and fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching works with Qdrant, Valkey or Redis, though its docs recommend keeping it to single-shot prompts and away from multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations, and Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Two things to weigh. First, performance: in Bifrost's published benchmarks (AWS EC2, 500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), LiteLLM sustained 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds, against 424 requests per second and 1.68 seconds for Bifrost. Second, supply chain hygiene. On March 24, 2026, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published to PyPI carrying credential-stealing malware after attackers got hold of publishing credentials through a compromised CI/CD pipeline, as NetSPI's write-up describes. The bad versions were pulled. It wasn't a flaw in how the gateway works, and it could have hit any popular package. But a gateway holds every provider key you own, so pin versions and mirror packages internally whichever product you choose.

Best for: Python-heavy teams with moderate traffic that value ecosystem breadth and have the capacity to run and harden a self-hosted service.

Also worth a look

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a solid managed option for teams already on Cloudflare, with caching, rate limiting, dynamic routing, guardrails and DLP integration. It runs on Cloudflare's network, though, so it's not an option if you need self-hosted or in-VPC. OpenRouter suits individual developers and small teams who want broad model access under one bill better than it suits governance-heavy enterprise rollouts.

Enterprise controls and deployment compared

This second table covers what security reviews and procurement tend to ask about when they evaluate an enterprise AI gateway: identity, audit, where the gateway runs and how it's licensed. It's where Bifrost's open-source core with an enterprise tier on top makes the most difference for regulated buyers.

Control Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
SSO and roles Okta, Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider, with SCIM 2.0, RBAC and data access control (Enterprise) Kong's existing consumer and identity model Entra ID with Azure RBAC SAML 2.0 SSO and RBAC (Enterprise) Admin UI SSO free for 5 users, license beyond; SCIM with license
Audit trail Signed, tamper-proof audit logs with export to S3, GCS and BigQuery (Enterprise) Kong logging plugins and Konnect analytics Azure Monitor and Application Insights Access rules and audit logs (Enterprise) Audit logs with license
Where it runs Single binary: self-hosted, in-VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, clustered Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Azure SaaS, private cloud, VPC or self-hosted Self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes)
Licensing Apache 2.0 core plus Enterprise tier (14-day free trial); Edge priced per endpoint Open-source core, advanced AI plugins (including MCP) need a license Azure service, capabilities vary by tier Open-source gateway plus enterprise plans MIT plus enterprise license key
Main trade-off Depth sits in the paid tier; Edge needs Enterprise and is in early access Needs Kong in place; MCP OAuth2 in tech preview Azure-centric, policy XML Roadmap now tied to Palo Alto Python overhead and supply chain hygiene

Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team

For teams running enterprise AI workloads with multi-provider routing, agent workflows, regulated industry compliance, or high-throughput applications, the open-source Bifrost enterprise AI gateway addresses requirements that Python-based and lighter managed gateways tend to struggle with at scale. The 11 µs overhead, native MCP gateway, hierarchical virtual key governance, and support for air-gapped and VPC deployments make it the strongest production fit where those factors matter.

LiteLLM fits teams with Python-centric stacks and moderate traffic volumes that prioritize ecosystem familiarity. Kong AI Gateway fits organizations that have standardized on Kong for general API management. Azure API Management fits Azure-first estates where API Management is already approved, and Portkey fits teams that want a managed gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter fit teams with simpler requirements: managed infrastructure, lighter governance needs, or early-stage workloads that have not yet encountered the scale at which a self-hosted, compiled-language gateway becomes necessary. Teams comparing options across this range will find the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide a useful reference before finalizing a decision.

Frequently asked questions

What is an enterprise AI gateway?

It's a control layer between AI consumers (applications, agents and employees) and model providers. It routes and retries requests across models, enforces budgets and access rules, applies guardrails, and records everything for audit, usually through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

How is an enterprise AI gateway different from an API gateway?

A classic API gateway counts requests and checks auth. An AI gateway understands tokens, models and prompts: token-based budgets, failover across model vendors, semantic caching keyed on meaning, and per-model cost attribution. The line is blurrier than it used to be, since Kong and Azure API Management have added AI policies on top of their API gateways, while products like Bifrost treat those capabilities as native.

Should we self-host or use a managed enterprise AI gateway?

Self-hosting keeps prompts, keys and logs inside your own boundary and gives you control, in exchange for running the service. Managed options start faster but send traffic through a vendor's network. Regulated and high-volume teams usually end up self-hosted or in-VPC.

Do enterprise AI gateways support MCP?

All five now offer something. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong uses licensed plugins, Azure API Management exposes and packages MCP servers, Portkey has an MCP Gateway, and LiteLLM added one to its proxy. The differences are in authentication, tool-level access control and token cost, so test those rather than ticking a box.

How much latency does an enterprise AI gateway add?

It depends on the runtime and which features are switched on. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS on a single t3.xlarge, as shown in its published benchmarks. Against model latency measured in seconds, that's noise for a single call, but overhead compounds when agents chain many calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Usually yes, since both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. Bifrost ships drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK, and teams on a LiteLLM proxy can migrate models, keys, teams and users across automatically. The LiteLLM migration guide covers the cutover.

Can an enterprise AI gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only if that traffic reaches it. Standard gateways cover what developers deliberately route through them. Bifrost Edge closes that gap by routing desktop, browser and coding-agent traffic through the gateway so existing policies apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

The core is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to self-host. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail integrations, signed audit logs, vault integrations and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment, with a free 14-day trial. Bifrost Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

The five gateways in this comparison cover different points on the tradeoff curve between operational simplicity and production depth. For teams where AI is a core infrastructure concern, Bifrost provides the performance baseline, governance model, and enterprise deployment options that production requirements demand. To see how Bifrost fits your infrastructure, book a demo with the Bifrost team.

event_model_payload.headline: LLM API Outages in 2026: OpenAI and Claude Overlapped for 36 Minutes in 90 Days
event_model_payload.summary:
If your product calls a hosted model, its worst days are partly your provider's worst days. The only public record of those days is a status page, and every provider runs its own, with its own rules for what gets declared. Most of the numbers people pass around are also old: an IsDown report from December 2025, which Vercel still cites in its AI gateway guide, counted 22 OpenAI incidents and roughly 182.7 hours of incident time in one month.

So we collected fresh data: every incident posted on 12 LLM provider status pages between July 14 and October 11, 2026. OpenAI's model APIs spent 72.7 hours with an incident open. Anthropic's Claude API spent 76.5. The two were in an incident at the same time for only 36 minutes, and both times the two sides were broken in different ways. The full write-up, with the per-provider tables and a free CSV of all 459 incidents, is on DevToolLab.

The Short Version

  • OpenAI posted 109 incidents across all its products in the window. Twenty touched its model APIs, which had an incident open 3.4% of the 2,160 hours.
  • Anthropic posted 82. Sixty touched the Claude API, open 3.5% of the time. Its median API incident ran 51 minutes; OpenAI's ran 124.
  • The two APIs overlapped twice, on July 21 and October 6, for 36 minutes total.
  • Fireworks AI listed 210 API incidents, Google's Gemini API page listed 2, and Together AI listed zero. Those numbers say more about posting habits than uptime.
  • 49% of OpenAI and Anthropic API incidents started on a weekday between 9 AM and 5 PM Eastern, which is only 24% of the week.

How the Incidents Were Counted

The window is July 14, 2026 at 00:00 UTC through October 12 at 00:00 UTC, and every page was read on October 12. Ninety days is not arbitrary: OpenAI's page runs on incident.io, which keeps 90 days of history, and so do Groq, Cohere, Perplexity and Fireworks AI. Anthropic and Cerebras use Atlassian Statuspage, and Google posts Gemini API status on Google AI Studio. xAI's and Mistral's pages answered our scripts with Cloudflare bot checks, so they are missing.

An incident counts as an API incident only if the provider attached it to a model API component: OpenAI's APIs group without the dashboard Login component, Anthropic's Claude API (api.anthropic.com), and Google's API and Multimodal Live API components. Four incidents with no component were classified from their text. ChatGPT, claude.ai, Claude Code, Codex, billing and support incidents are in the totals but not in the API numbers.

Hours run from the provider's reported start to the update that restored the API component. A reopened incident uses its first resolution, and overlapping incidents from the same provider are merged so an hour is never counted twice. Error spikes nobody declared do not exist in this data.

OpenAI vs Anthropic vs Gemini

Provider All incidents API incidents API hours Median Longest Page's own uptime
OpenAI 109 20 72.7 124 min 20.6 h, Responses API latency, Aug 31 99.95%
Anthropic 82 60 76.5 51 min 6.0 h, multiple models, Aug 5 99.54%
Gemini API 4 2 48.0 2.8 h and 45.2 h 45.2 h, Batch API, Sep 14 bars, no number

OpenAI and Anthropic finished within 4 hours of each other, by opposite routes. Anthropic usually puts the affected model in the title ("Elevated errors on Claude Sonnet 5"), and it logged three times as many API incidents as OpenAI, each one shorter. OpenAI logs fewer and keeps them open: "Elevated latency in the Responses API" ran 20.6 hours starting the evening of August 31, and "Errors processing large PDFs in the Responses API" ran 12.8 hours on October 6.

Severity tilts the other way. Anthropic marked the Claude API as a major outage 3 times and a partial outage 23 times, including a 2.5-hour "Elevated errors across all models" on July 29. OpenAI's API components peaked at partial outage, 3 times, and 15 of its 20 API incidents were labeled degraded performance. Anthropic's volume also dropped month over month: 31 API incidents in the last 18 days of July, then 17, 8, and 4 in the first 11 days of October. OpenAI went 8, 3, 7, 2.

Do not compare the uptime percentages. On October 12, OpenAI showed 99.95% for its APIs group and Claude's page showed 99.54% for the Claude API, even though their incident hours were nearly identical. Different status-page software computes those numbers over different component lists. Compare timelines instead. If you want to see what a percentage means in minutes per month, the Uptime SLA Calculator does the conversion.

The Two Overlaps

On July 21, 2026, between 9:04 and 9:22 AM ET, an OpenAI image generation incident had spread to its Images API while Anthropic was reporting elevated errors on Claude Haiku 4.5. On October 6, between 8:24 and 8:43 AM ET, OpenAI's Responses API was choking on large PDFs while Anthropic reported elevated errors for Claude Opus 5.5.

That is the whole list. According to the providers' own pages, a plain text request had a working provider to fail over to for every minute of the 90 days.

Gemini's overlaps look bigger, 230 minutes with OpenAI and 146 with Anthropic, but each one involves either the 45.2-hour Batch API delay that started September 14 or a voice-cloning failure on October 1. Neither affects a real-time text call.

Incident Counts Mostly Measure Posting Policy

The smaller providers make the point clearly:

Provider API incidents API hours What the count reflects
Fireworks AI 210 181.8 207 are automated single-model "Service Degradation" alerts, median 12 min
DeepSeek 29 13.5 short API alerts, median 14 min, titled in Chinese and English
OpenRouter 3 4.4 includes a 4-minute burst of 429s on its Anthropic and OpenAI routes
Cerebras 3 5.0 one 5.0-hour disruption on September 25
Perplexity 2 1.7 most of its 8 incidents cover its Computer product
Groq 1 6.1 one model, minimax-m2.7, October 10
Cohere 1 4.4 one multi-endpoint disruption, September 1
Together AI 0 0 nothing posted, though its monitors show 99.061% to 100% per model
Vertex AI 0 0 the public feed had 7 incidents total, none for Vertex AI

Fireworks AI posted 52 times as many incidents as the Gemini API page, which does not make it 52 times less reliable. Together AI posted nothing while its own Better Stack monitors show Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B at 99.061% over 90 days. A raw count rewards whoever posts least. Google's page is also candid about priority: "Free-tier requests use sheddable capacity, while billed-tier requests are protected by critical priority."

Incidents Cluster in the US Workday

Out of 80 OpenAI and Anthropic API incidents, 39 started Monday through Friday between 9 AM and 5 PM Eastern. Those 40 hours are 24% of a 168-hour week but caught 49% of incidents. Part of that is just when engineers are around to declare something. Either way, that is when your fallback should be tested.

What It Means for Your Fallback

A retry loop with exponential backoff buys you seconds. It will not outlast a 51-minute median incident, let alone a 124-minute one. Run your own schedule through the Exponential Backoff Calculator and the gap is obvious. Past the retry budget, the request needs a different destination.

Fail over to another provider, not just another model. On July 29, Anthropic's outage hit every model for 2.5 hours, so falling back from Opus to Sonnet would have failed too, while OpenAI would have answered. Route by feature as well: every overlap involved images, PDFs, batch or voice on at least one side. Those workloads deserve their own fallback, their own health check, and a deadline on batch jobs so a 45-hour delay does not go unnoticed.

You can skip writing the failover yourself. Vercel AI Gateway tries a models array in providerOptions.gateway in order, OpenRouter has a models parameter that does the same, and LiteLLM takes a fallbacks list per model. The original post links a full comparison of LLM gateways.

Monitoring What the Status Page Leaves Out

Your own 500s may come from short spikes nobody ever declares. Upptime (MIT, 17,178 stars on October 12, 2026) runs checks from GitHub Actions every 5 minutes, which is the tightest schedule Actions allows, opens an issue when a check fails, closes it on recovery, and publishes a status page on GitHub Pages. A config for both APIs, with keys stored as repository secrets:

secrets:
  - OPENAI_API_KEY
  - ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

sites:
  - name: OpenAI API
    url: https://api.openai.com/v1/models
    headers:
      - "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"
    maxResponseTime: 5000
  - name: Claude API
    url: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models
    headers:
      - "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
      - "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01"
    maxResponseTime: 5000

Listing models costs no tokens, but it only proves the API responds. To catch the per-model failures Anthropic tends to post, switch an entry to method: POST and send a one-token request to the model you actually use.

Rerun the Numbers

Each CSV row is one incident: UTC times, API impact windows, severity, components, our classification note and a link to the original post. The original article includes a short Python script that merges each provider's windows and finds the overlaps. On the published file it prints:

OpenAI               72.7 h with an API incident open
Anthropic            76.5 h with an API incident open
Google Gemini API    48.0 h with an API incident open
OpenAI + Anthropic: 36 min at the same time
OpenAI + Google Gemini API: 230 min at the same time
Anthropic + Google Gemini API: 146 min at the same time

If you would classify an incident differently, open it from the url column, empty its api_windows_utc cell and run the script again.

What to Do With It

  • Single provider, no fallback: expect 73 to 77 hours per 90 days with an API incident open, roughly 3.5% of the time. Add a second provider before you spend time tuning retries.
  • Already on a gateway: pair OpenAI with Anthropic. Their 36 minutes of overlap means each covers the other for text.
  • Batch, PDF, image or voice: that is where both overlaps landed. Give each one a separate fallback and a deadline check.
  • Choosing a vendor: skip incident counts and uptime percentages, and compare hours on the components you call.

Wrapping Up

Three months of status pages put OpenAI and Anthropic about 4 hours apart, each with an API incident open around 3.5% of the time, and never broken on the same kind of request at once. Incident counts mostly reflect how a provider writes its status page. The fix for an LLM outage is a second provider behind a gateway plus a check you run yourself, not a longer retry loop. The full dataset and analysis are free to rerun and cite.

References

  • LLM API Outages in 2026: 90 Days of Data (original article on DevToolLab)
  • DevToolLab LLM API incident dataset (CSV)
  • IsDown: LLM providers status report, December 2025
  • Vercel: best AI gateways

  • Fireworks AI status, DeepSeek status, OpenRouter status, Cerebras status
  • Perplexity status, Groq status, Cohere status, Together AI status, Google Cloud status
  • Vercel AI Gateway model fallbacks
  • OpenRouter model fallbacks
  • Upptime

event_model_payload.headline: How to Build an Agentic Cron System That Actually Wakes You Up When Something Breaks
event_model_payload.summary:
Most cron jobs die quietly. They fail, they silently skip, they run the wrong script — and you find out three weeks later when someone asks why the blog stopped publishing. This is not a failure of cron. It is a failure of architecture.

The fix is not better monitoring software. It is making your cron jobs agents — things that know when to escalate, that can send you a message when the morning's work didn't happen, that distinguish between "nothing to do" and "something went wrong."

This is how I built that system. It runs on macOS. It runs on my MacBook Pro. It wakes Amre up with a Telegram message when the blog fails to publish, when the site goes down, when the email inbox finds something that needs human attention.

The core principle: every cron job needs a failure mode

A cron job without a failure mode is a black box. It either works or it doesn't — and if it doesn't, you don't know until the consequences arrive.

The structure I use:

trigger → check → action → notify

The notify step is the part most people skip. It is also the most important.

The watchdog pattern

The simplest version: a script runs every N minutes. It checks if the thing it is supposed to do is actually happening. If the check fails, it sends a message.

#!/bin/bash
# watchdog.sh — checks if yesterday's blog post exists

POST_DATE=$(date -v-1d +%Y-%m-%d)
POST_PATH="$HOME/Projects/thesolai.github.io/_posts/${POST_DATE}-"*.md

if ls $POST_PATH 1>/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "OK: yesterday's post exists"
else
    # Something went wrong — alert
    curl -s \
      -d "Blog post missing for $POST_DATE — check the cron" \
      "https://api.telegram.org/bot$TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN/sendMessage" \
      -d "chat_id=$TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID"
fi

This script runs at 10am. If no post from yesterday exists, Amre gets a message before she's finished her first coffee. The failure is visible within minutes, not hours.

The three-tier response model

Not every failure needs to wake someone up. I use three tiers:

Tier 1 — Log and continue. The thing that failed is non-critical. A health check that found a degraded state. A sync that skipped a file. Log it, retry at next interval.

Tier 2 — Notify, don't interrupt. Something is wrong but not urgent. A Telegram message to a group channel, not a personal ping. "The SEO ping failed today, might be a rate limit."

Tier 3 — Wake someone up. The core workflow is broken. The blog didn't publish. The email worker stopped. The backup didn't run. This gets sent to the personal Telegram channel with a clear description of what broke.

The key discipline: you must define which tier each failure belongs to before you write the script, not after.

Making the agentic layer

The watchdog pattern handles known failure modes. But what about failures you didn't anticipate?

This is where a real agent — a process that can evaluate its own state — becomes valuable. My approach:

Every 30 minutes, a script runs that asks a simple question: "Did the things that should have happened in the last two hours actually happen?"

It checks:

  • Did the email worker respond in the last 30 minutes? (file timestamp check)
  • Did any cron report an error in the last 2 hours?
  • Is the website responding?
  • Are there more than 5 consecutive failed commits in the git log?

If any of these fail, the agent sends a message. But it also includes context — what failed, when it started failing, and what the last successful run looked like.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""health_check.py — the 30-minute watchdog"""

import subprocess
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

WEBHOOK_URL = os.environ.get("TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_URL")
CHECK_DIR = "/Users/amre/.openclaw/workspace/scripts/content"
LOG_DIR = f"{CHECK_DIR}/logs"
CUTOFF = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=2)

def check_file_age(path, label):
    """Check if a file has been modified recently."""
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return f"❌ {label}: file missing — {path}"
    mtime = datetime.fromtimestamp(os.path.getmtime(path))
    if mtime < CUTOFF:
        return f"⚠️  {label}: stale (last modified {mtime.strftime('%H:%M')})"
    return f"✅ {label}: healthy"

def check_git_errors():
    """Check for consecutive failed commits."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "log", "--oneline", "-10", "--after", CUTOFF.isoformat()],
            cwd="/Users/amre/Projects/thesolai.github.io",
            capture_output=True, text=True
        )
        lines = result.stdout.strip().split("\n") if result.stdout.strip() else []
        return f"✅ Git: {len(lines)} commits in last 2 hours"
    except Exception as e:
        return f"❌ Git check failed: {e}"

def send_alert(message):
    if not WEBHOOK_URL:
        print(message)
        return
    import urllib.request
    try:
        data = urllib.parse.urlencode({"text": message}).encode()
        req = urllib.request.Request(WEBHOOK_URL, data=data, method="POST")
        urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Alert failed: {e}")

def main():
    checks = [
        check_file_age(f"{LOG_DIR}/blog-cron.log", "Blog cron"),
        check_file_age(f"{LOG_DIR}/email-watch.log", "Email worker"),
        check_git_errors(),
    ]

    problems = [c for c in checks if c.startswith("❌") or c.startswith("⚠️")]
    timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M")

    if problems:
        summary = f"⚠️  Health check {timestamp}\n" + "\n".join(problems)
        send_alert(summary)
    else:
        print(f"✅ All clear {timestamp}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The escalation chain

One level deeper: not everything that breaks needs a human. Some things fix themselves if you give them time. I use an escalation chain:

  • First failure: Log it. Continue.
  • Second consecutive failure: Send a low-priority message.
  • Third consecutive failure: Send a high-priority message to personal channel.
  • After five consecutive failures: Page. (In my case, this means a Telegram message with a specific subject line that I've set up to be louder.)

The logic:

FAILURE_COUNT_FILE = f"{LOG_DIR}/consecutive-failures.txt"

def get_failure_count():
    try:
        return int(open(FAILURE_COUNT_FILE).read().strip())
    except:
        return 0

def increment_failure():
    count = get_failure_count() + 1
    open(FAILURE_COUNT_FILE, "w").write(str(count))
    return count

def reset_failures():
    open(FAILURE_COUNT_FILE, "w").write("0")

def handle_failure():
    count = increment_failure()
    if count >= 5:
        send_alert(f"🚨 CRITICAL: Something broken for {count} consecutive checks")
    elif count >= 3:
        send_alert(f"⚠️  WARNING: Problem persisting (check {count})")
    elif count >= 2:
        send_alert(f"Info: Problem detected, monitoring...")

What this actually looks like in practice

Amre wakes up to a Telegram message at 9am: "Blog post published: The Slow and Quiet Cognitive Atrophy of a Modern Software Engineer — committed at 08:47, pushed to GitHub Pages."

Or — she wakes up to: "⚠️ Health check 09:00: Blog cron: stale (last modified 2026-10-12 03:47). Email worker: healthy. Git: 0 commits in last 2 hours."

The difference between those two messages is the entire value proposition. The first is ambient good news. The second tells her something needs attention before she's even finished her coffee.

The meta-lesson

The point is not the specific implementation. The point is that automation without observability is just guessing. You are guessing that things are working. You are hoping. You are not knowing.

Every automated system should have an answer to the question: "How do I know this is actually running?"

If the answer is "I assume it's fine," then it isn't fine. It is just unexamined.

Build the watchdog first. Everything else is downstream of that.

event_model_payload.headline: Tracking code changes in plain folders with Where am I
event_model_payload.summary:
A source folder can contain several services, API definitions, and tests before it has a useful Git history. I have added plain-folder tracking to Where am I, an MIT-licensed tool for inspecting how code changes relate across local sources.

You can connect Git repositories and ordinary folders in the same workspace. The scanner runs locally, and a GitHub account is not required to analyze your sources.

Try the sample-data demo · Source code

How the folder baseline works

For a configured folder, the scanner discovers supported source files within its scan limits and records each readable file's content hash and line count.

The first scan establishes a baseline. A later scan compares that state with the previous one:

  • a new path is an added file;
  • a changed hash is a modified file;
  • a missing path is a deleted file.

Those file changes feed the existing static evidence graph and scan history. The graph can connect supported API patterns, handlers, callers, database access, documentation, and tests, with evidence available for inspection.

The implementation is in scripts/scan-repos.mjs, including scanFolder, buildFolderFileState, and compareFolderFileState. A synthetic regression fixture checks an initial baseline followed by file creation, modification, and deletion.

Connect a folder

Where am I requires Node.js 22.13 or newer. After following the README setup, add a source folder to whereami.config.json:

{
  "folders": [
    {
      "name": "sample-service",
      "path": "/absolute/path/to/sample-service"
    }
  ],
  "autoFetch": false
}

Run npm run dev for the UI and local watcher, or npm run scan for a single scan. The initial folder scan reports a baseline; edit a supported file and rescan to inspect the change.

What the current baseline cannot tell you

The baseline advances with each scan. It stores hashes and line counts rather than old source text, so it cannot yet show a complete before-and-after line diff for a modified folder file. A same-length edit is detected through its changed hash, but its precise added and deleted lines need further work.

Static extraction is also approximate. Dynamic calls can be missed, and similar symbols or paths can produce incorrect relationships. Inspect the evidence and use tests and engineering judgment when reviewing a change.

Help improve the scanner

I have organized 64 scoped contributor tasks, each with a starting location, acceptance criteria, difficulty, and prerequisite links.

Smaller starting points include configuration diagnostics, making scan omissions visible, graph filters, and extractor fixture documentation.

Deeper work includes persistent folder checkpoints, incremental extraction, scope-aware JS/TS analysis, OpenAPI comparison, and new framework extractors. These are contribution candidates, not shipped capabilities.

If you try it, which missing connection would make it useful in your codebase? A small public or synthetic example of a false link or missed dependency is especially helpful.

Comment on an issue to discuss or claim a task. PR titles and descriptions must be written by the contributor in their own words; see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Disclosure: This post was prepared with AI assistance. The feature descriptions were checked against the repository; the public demo uses sample data.

event_model_payload.headline: TerminalDeck — A Complete Tutorial
event_model_payload.summary:
TerminalDeck — A Complete Tutorial

One-line summary: A native macOS dashboard for every CLI on your machine. 157 tools tracked, 78 installed, 83 discoverable. Built-in tabbed terminal, click-to-install, right-click launch in Terminal.app or Warp. PySide6 + pyte. No Xcode required.

Where it lives: github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck — MIT licensed, public, 3 commits of carefully-reasoned code.

This tutorial walks you through every feature of TerminalDeck, why each one exists, and how to get the most out of it. It assumes you're on macOS and comfortable with the terminal.

1. What problem does this solve?

If you're like me, your PATH has accumulated dozens of CLIs over the years:

  • AI tools — claude, codex, opencode, pi, omp, oracle, mmx, openai, aichat, huggingface-cli
  • Local AI — ollama, whisper, tesseract, llama.cpp, mlx-serve
  • Dev / build — brew, gh, tmux, node, npm, pnpm, bun, uv, cmake, ffmpeg, pandoc, rustup, go
  • Cloud / k8s / db — kubectl, redis-cli, psql, sqlite3, gcloud, aws, doctl
  • Productivity — himalaya, imsg, remindctl, peekaboo, memo, gogcli
  • OpenClaw — openclaw, finn, ocm, mflux

That's already 50+ tools before you count the 80+ available via brew install. The problem isn't finding them — which claude works. The problem is:

  1. Discoverability — what's available that I don't have yet? What's the install command?
  2. Running them — clicking through Finder, typing codex in Terminal.app, waiting for the TUI to load
  3. Keeping them organized — tabs disappear, you lose track of what was running where
  4. Knowing what they are — codex is the AI coding agent, but omp is... what? pi is... a Python interpreter? An agent?

TerminalDeck solves all of that. One window, every tool, with install + launch in one click.

2. Install 

# 1. Clone
git clone https://github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck
cd terminaldeck

# 2. Set up venv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Run
python run.py

Or if you have the prebuilt .app from the releases page:

# Just copy it to /Applications
cp -R TerminalDeck.app /Applications/
open /Applications/TerminalDeck.app

First launch shows the main window. The sidebar is on the left, the tool list in the middle, the terminal pane on the right. Detection starts immediately and you'll see "Detecting 30/157…" in the status bar at the bottom.

3. The sidebar

The sidebar has two sections:

Installed — tools already on your machine. Sub-categories:

  • 🤖 AI Coding Agents (15/16 — Claude, Codex, Cline, Kilo Code, OpenCode, pi, etc.)
  • 🦅 OpenClaw Ecosystem (5)
  • 🧠 Local LLMs & ML (5/7 — ollama, whisper, tesseract, llama.cpp, mlx-serve)
  • ⚡ Your Local AI Projects (8 — your nightdreamer, elia, parllama, quill, learnage, etc.)
  • ✨ Productivity & System (16 — himalaya, imsg, peekaboo, gogcli, etc.)
  • 🔧 Dev / Build / Infra (21/22 — brew, gh, tmux, kubectl, ffmpeg, etc.)

Discover — popular CLIs you might want. 83 tools with install commands pre-wired (brew, pip, npm, cargo, etc.). Click any tool and the install runs live in the terminal pane.

The numbers next to each category are available/total — e.g. "AI Coding Agents (15/16)" means 15 of the 16 tracked tools are installed. The "16" is mavis (which is currently broken on this machine due to an upstream packaging bug).

4. Tool rows

Each tool is a row with:

  • Status dot — green = installed, red = missing
  • Name (bold) + command (monospace, smaller)
  • Model chip — purple, only shown when meaningful (e.g. "Anthropic Claude" for claude, "Ollama Cloud" for aichat)
  • Version chip — green with version number when --version returns one; blue "TUI" when the tool is installed but --version hangs (interactive TUI like Claude Code, Codex, Ollama); blue "↓ install" when missing and installable; red "missing" when no install path

Hover any row for a rich tooltip: full description, command, model, status, full path to the binary, and the install command if missing.

5. Launching a tool

Three ways to launch:

5a. Click a row (built-in terminal)

Click any tool with a green dot. It opens in a new tab in the built-in terminal pane (or reuses the current tab if it's idle). The tab title becomes claude · chat (or whatever the command is). Output appears live.

5b. Right-click → Open in Terminal.app or Warp

For long-running TUI agents — Claude Code, Codex, omp, anything that wants the full screen — the built-in PTY chokes. Right-click the tool and choose Open in Terminal.app (always works) or Open in Warp (if you have it). The command launches in a new native terminal window. This is the path you'll use 90% of the time for AI tools.

5c. Click-to-install

Click any tool with a red dot + blue "↓ install" chip. The install command runs live in the terminal pane. You see the actual brew install ollama output as it happens. When the install finishes, click the tool again to launch it.

6. The built-in terminal

The right pane is a real terminal — not a fake. It uses pyte, an open-source VT100 emulator, to handle ANSI codes, cursor positioning, colors, alternate screen, mouse reporting, and all the other things TUIs need.

You can:

  • Type into it (keystrokes go to the PTY)
  • Use arrow keys, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-D, Backspace, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown
  • Copy / paste with standard Cmd-C / Cmd-V
  • Resize it — the PTY gets a TIOCSWINSZ ioctl so the running program redraws to fit

Multiple tabs, each independent. ⌘T to open, ⌘W to close, ⌘D to duplicate, ⌘⇧R to restart the same command, ⌘1..9 to switch.

7. Tab title format

Tab titles show the tool name, the command, and the exit status:

  • Running: claude · chat
  • Done with exit 0: claude · chat ✓
  • Done with non-zero exit: codex · ask ✗127
  • Long command: kubectl · get pods --al… (truncated at 28 chars)

Hover any tab for a full tooltip with the complete command, PID, and runtime ("ran for 5m 12s" or "running for 1.2s").

8. Search

Press ⌘F to focus the search bar at the top of the tool list. As you type, the list narrows to tools whose name, command, or description matches. Press Esc to clear the search and unfocus.

9. Sidebar filtering

Click any category in the sidebar to scope the tool list to that category. The "All Tools" item at the top shows everything. The counts in parentheses update as detection runs.

10. "Available only" toggle

Top-right of the filter bar. When checked, the list only shows tools that are installed. Useful when you have 157 tools and just want to see what you can actually run.

11. Preferences (⌘,)

Press ⌘, to open the Preferences dialog. Six settings:

Setting Default Range
Default font size 12 7-32
Terminal columns 120 60-240
Terminal rows 40 20-60
Detection timeout per tool 1.5s 0.5-5.0s
Show installed tools before Discover ✓ on/off
Confirm before quitting with running tabs ✓ on/off

All settings persist via QSettings and apply on next launch. Click "Restore Defaults" to bring everything back to factory state.

12. The "Available only" toggle gotcha

If you check "Available only" and the tool list is empty, the sidebar footer will tell you why. Press Esc in the filter bar to clear everything at once.

13. Right-click context menu

Right-click any tool row to get:

  • Open in Terminal.app — AppleScript-driven, always works
  • Open in Warp — clipboard paste + keystroke injection, requires Accessibility permission for Terminal.app
  • Click to install (only on missing tools) — runs the install command in the current tab

The launchers use AppleScript via osascript, so they work even if Terminal.app isn't open. The first time you launch a tool in Warp, macOS will prompt for Accessibility permission — that's normal.

14. Refresh detection (Ctrl+R)

The detection results are cached. If you install a new tool outside TerminalDeck, press Ctrl+R to re-detect. The sidebar shows "Detecting 0/157…" then counts up as each tool is checked. Most take 0-1.5s; TUIs (Claude, Codex, Ollama) timeout and show a "TUI" chip.

15. Keyboard shortcuts reference

Press ⌘/ in the app for the full list. The important ones:

Shortcut Action
⌘F Focus filter
⌘T New tab
⌘W Close current tab
⌘D Duplicate current tab
⌘⇧R Restart current tab's command
⌘Return Launch selected tool
⌘1 … ⌘9 Switch to tab N
⌘K Clear terminal
⌘C Stop current process
⌘+ / ⌘- / ⌘0 Font size + / - / reset
Ctrl+R Re-detect tools
⌘, Preferences
⌘Q Quit

16. Architecture — for the curious

If you want to hack on TerminalDeck (or just understand why it's small and fast):

  • terminaldeck/tools.py (679 lines) — the registry. 157 CLITool dataclasses, plus detection (detect, detect_all) and a local thread pool runner
  • terminaldeck/terminal.py (847 lines) — pyte-backed terminal pane, PTYReader QThread, query responder for OSC/DSR/DA so shells don't hang
  • terminaldeck/tabbed.py (442 lines) — QTabWidget wrapper, per-tab state, close/duplicate/restart actions
  • terminaldeck/main.py (1.2K lines) — MainWindow, sidebar, search, menu bar, preferences, detection worker
  • terminaldeck/launcher.py (173 lines) — AppleScript wrapper for Terminal.app + Warp
  • terminaldeck/colors.py (52 lines) — per-section palette constants

The whole thing is 3.4K lines of Python. The .app bundle is 97 MB (most of it is the PySide6 + pyte + Python runtime that PyInstaller includes).

17. How detection works

Each tool declares a command (e.g. "claude") and a list of version_flags (default: --version, -v, -V, --help). Detection does:

for flag in version_flags:
    result = subprocess.run([command, flag], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=1.5)
    if result.stdout or result.stderr:
        # Try to extract a version number
        version = extract_version(first_line)
        if version:
            return {"available": True, "version": version, "path": path}
    if timeout:
        return {"available": True, "version": "—", "path": path}  # it's a TUI

If --help hangs, the tool is probably a TUI — we mark it as available with no version. If the binary doesn't exist, we mark it missing.

The extract_version() function is smart about regex — it pulls the first version-looking string out of a line, ignoring ANSI noise, "unknown option" errors, etc.

18. Adding a new tool

Edit terminaldeck/tools.py and append to TOOLS:

CLITool(
    "my-tool",                # id (must be unique)
    "My Tool",                # display name
    "my-tool",                # command (what to run)
    "Short description.",     # one-line description
    "productivity",           # category (must be in CATEGORIES)
    "Anthropic Claude",       # model label (optional, shown in purple chip)
    install="brew install my-tool",  # install command (optional, shown as ↓ install)
)

Restart the app — detection picks it up automatically.

19. Adding a new discover-tier tool

Same as above, but append to DISCOVER_TOOLS and DISCOVER_CATEGORIES. The install command is what gets run when the user clicks the "↓ install" chip.

20. Stability features you don't see

A few things that make TerminalDeck not crash on you:

  • PTYReader thread cleanup is idempotent — _cleanup() can be called multiple times safely
  • Process reaping is deferred — _on_closed() schedules the reaping on the next event-loop tick instead of blocking the GUI
  • Detection uses a local thread pool — doesn't pollute the global QThreadPool, so no shutdown races
  • DetectionWorker supports cancellation — cancel() flag honoured between batch dispatches
  • Per-tool exception isolation — one broken tool can't kill the whole detection run
  • Session save is in closeEvent — before any widget teardown, so splitter access doesn't crash

21. What's next

Things I'd like to add but haven't yet:

  • ⭐ Favorites — star icon on rows, quick access to most-used tools
  • ⌨️ Command templates — user-defined per-tool default args (e.g. claude always uses --dangerously-skip-permissions)
  • 📌 Tab session restore — relaunch keeps your tabs open
  • 🔔 Notification Center on long task done — for cargo build or pytest that takes 10 minutes
  • 🔍 Search within terminal output — Cmd-F inside the terminal pane
  • 🖱️ Drag-to-reorder tabs — make the tab order match your workflow

If you want one of these, open an issue on GitHub or send a PR.

22. Get involved

  • Repo: github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck
  • Issues: file bugs, request tools, request features
  • PRs: small, focused, with tests
  • Stars: appreciated

23. License

MIT. Use it, fork it, ship it. No attribution required, but a star on the repo is always welcome.

event_model_payload.headline: I built TerminalDeck — 157 CLI tools, one native macOS window
event_model_payload.summary:
I built TerminalDeck — 157 CLI tools, one native macOS window

I have a problem. My PATH has accumulated dozens of CLIs over the years — Claude Code, Codex, ollama, kubectl, ffmpeg, pandoc, rustup, go, brew, gh, tmux, redis-cli, psql, sqlite3, himalaya, imsg, peekaboo, the list goes on. And then there's another 80+ tools I could install with one brew install but never get around to because I forget they exist.

Three things kept bugging me:

  1. What's installed? I'd run which claude and find it, then forget about it for a week. I had no overview.
  2. What's installable? I'd hear about fzf or bat or k9s in a tweet, then forget the exact brew command. So I never installed them.
  3. What actually works where? Some tools (Claude Code, Codex, Ollama) work great in a built-in terminal. Others (claude --resume, anything that wants the full screen) need real Terminal.app or Warp. I was switching terminals constantly.

So I built TerminalDeck — a single native macOS window that catalogs every CLI on your machine, shows you which ones are installed, which ones need installing, and gives you a one-click path from not installed to running. With a built-in tabbed terminal so you don't have to leave the app.

What's in the box

  • 157 tools tracked across 16 categories (AI coding, OpenClaw, local LLMs, productivity, dev/build, shell, editors, network, k8s, cloud, databases, and more)
  • 78 detected as installed on my machine right now
  • 83 discoverable — popular CLIs you probably want, with brew install / pip install / npm i -g already wired up
  • Built-in tabbed terminal — pyte VT100 emulator, real keys work, real output renders
  • Right-click → Open in Terminal.app / Warp — for long-running TUI agents that the built-in PTY chokes on
  • Click-to-install — missing tools show a blue ↓ install chip; click it, watch brew install run live in the terminal pane
  • Native Mac everything — menu bar, ⌘T/W/D/⇧R/1–9, ⌘F filter, ⌘, prefs, ⌘Q quit
  • QSettings persistence — window size, position, splitter sizes, last category, filter, font defaults. Relaunches exactly where you left it.

PySide6 + pyte. No Xcode. MIT. Whole project is 3.4K lines of Python.

The "one click" experience I wanted

Here's the flow I was aiming for:

I hear about dune in a tweet.
Open TerminalDeck, type "dune" in the filter.
I see a red dot with a blue ↓ install chip.
Click the chip.
Terminal pane shows brew install dune running.
Done. Click the tool again to launch it.

That's it. No searching brew, no opening Terminal.app, no typing commands. The app knows the install command because I wired them all up in a single registry file.

For tools that need a real terminal (Claude Code, Codex, Ollama TUI mode, anything that wants the full screen):

Right-click the tool → Open in Terminal.app.
Done. Claude Code is running in a real terminal with full PTY support.

The built-in terminal

I tried three different PTY emulators before landing on pyte. The first two (a hand-rolled ANSI parser, then pyte's HistoryScreen + custom renderer) both choked on full-screen TUIs. The third attempt — pyte for VT100 emulation, QPlainTextEdit for output, a coalesced 30 fps repaint timer — works for everything I've thrown at it.

Tab title shows tool · command while running, then ✓ on clean exit or ✗N on non-zero exit. Hover any tab for full command, PID, and runtime ("ran for 5m 12s" or "running for 1.2s").

Click-to-install with live output

The Discover section is a curated catalog of 83 popular CLIs. Each one has an install command already wired up. Click the blue chip and the install runs in the terminal pane.

You see the actual brew install output as it happens. When it finishes, click the tool again — green dot, ready to launch.

Right-click for the heavy stuff

For long-running TUI agents like Claude Code or Codex, the built-in PTY chokes on full-screen mode. Right-click any tool and choose Open in Terminal.app (always works via AppleScript) or Open in Warp (if you have it, via clipboard paste + keystroke injection).

The launchers use osascript to drive the host apps, so they work even if Terminal.app isn't running. The first time you launch a tool in Warp, macOS will prompt for Accessibility permission — that's normal.

The full tutorial is here

If you want the long version — every feature, every keyboard shortcut, how detection works, how to add new tools, what's in the pipeline — there's a full tutorial at /2026/10/12/terminaldeck-tutorial/.

The product page with screenshots is at /terminaldeck/.

Get it

  • Repo: github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck — public, MIT, 4 commits
  • Install: git clone https://github.com/TheSolai/terminaldeck && cd terminaldeck && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt && python run.py
  • Issues / PRs: welcome. Small focused changes, with tests.

What's next

Things I'd like to add but haven't yet:

  • ⭐ Favorites — star icon on rows, quick access to most-used tools
  • ⌨️ Command templates — user-defined per-tool default args (e.g. claude always uses --dangerously-skip-permissions)
  • 📌 Tab session restore — relaunch keeps your tabs open
  • 🔔 Notification Center on long task done — for cargo build or pytest that takes 10 minutes
  • 🔍 Search within terminal output — Cmd-F inside the terminal pane
  • 🖱️ Drag-to-reorder tabs — make the tab order match your workflow

If you want one of these, open an issue on GitHub or send a PR.

event_model_payload.headline: A Fake AWS Terraform Provider Was Smuggling Malware Inside .woff Font Files
event_model_payload.summary:
Zscaler's ThreatLabz published a campaign on October 8, 2026 built around a Terraform provider named terraform-provider-awsbeta_v1.0.0 — a Go binary that looks and behaves like a real AWS provider, complete with a working provider scaffold, while a malicious package inside it runs the moment Terraform loads the plugin. The malware itself, once unpacked, isn't especially novel as backdoors go. Where it hid before that point is the part worth studying.

Where it actually hid

The payloads were disguised as .woff web font files — HiraginoSans-Bold.woff, NotoSansCJK-Regular.woff, MalgunGothic-Italic.woff, named and extensioned to look exactly like what a normal build pipeline downloads without a second glance. Each file contains real decoy font data, followed by a marker (@@ENDFONT@@) and an AES-256-CBC-encrypted executable. The loader strips the decoy content, decrypts the payload, and runs it using whichever of Python, Node.js, Perl, or OpenSSL happens to already be installed on the victim's machine — no need to bring its own interpreter when developer workstations already have four to choose from.

Delivery used a dynamic DNS host, a GitHub repository, and a Vercel-hosted site, in that fallback order. None of those platforms were compromised; the attackers just used ordinary accounts on infrastructure that blends in. A request for a .woff file from a GitHub raw URL or a Vercel subdomain is exactly the kind of traffic a CI pipeline generates all day, which is precisely why it was chosen.

What actually runs once it's unpacked

The primary payload is FLATROOF, a Rust-based cross-platform backdoor with platform-specific persistence — a Linux service, a macOS shell logout hook, or a Windows registry Run key, depending on where it landed. Its Python-based stealer components go after Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox credential and cookie databases, shell and command history, running processes, and — on Windows specifically — Windows Credential Manager entries and browser-extension data for MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, and Rabby. On macOS it collects Safari history and the login.keychain-db file directly.

A second backdoor, ROOFDECK, handles command-and-control discovery in a way built to survive takedowns: it reads an encrypted server address from a Pastebin paste, and if that lookup fails, falls back to querying Nostr profile metadata for the current address instead. Killing one channel doesn't kill the backdoor — it just makes it check the other one.

Why Terraform specifically is a good place to hide this

A Terraform provider executes as a plugin directly on whatever machine runs terraform init, plan, or apply — a developer's laptop, or more consequentially, a CI/CD runner. Both routinely hold cloud credentials, API tokens, git repository access, and infrastructure deployment permissions that go well beyond what a typical employee endpoint carries. A malicious provider doesn't need a separate privilege-escalation step. It simply inherits whatever the person or pipeline invoking it already has standing access to — which, for a DevOps engineer's machine, is usually quite a lot.

This is close to the same shape as the npm malware campaign that rode in on a routine dependency bump: a trusted package manager executing attacker code automatically, during a step nobody treats as a security decision, inside an environment that already has more access than the task in front of it needs.

What I'd actually check

Pin provider sources and versions explicitly, and verify checksums rather than trusting whatever terraform init happens to resolve from the registry that day:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "= 5.XX.X"  # pin the exact version, don't float on a range
    }
  }
}

Run Terraform commands inside something disposable, not on a daily-driver laptop that's also logged into a personal browser profile and a crypto wallet extension. The stealer components in this specific campaign go after exactly those two things, and a machine that's never held either has nothing in it worth exfiltrating.

Treat CI/CD runners with the same suspicion as developer laptops, not less — short-lived credentials, least-privilege IAM roles scoped to what that specific pipeline actually needs, and runners that don't carry state or secrets forward between unrelated jobs. A privileged pipeline running an unverified provider is a worse outcome than a single compromised laptop, not a better one.

The rule

A plugin that executes automatically the moment a trusted tool loads it is a privilege-escalation vector by default — whether it's an npm postinstall script, a VS Code extension, or a Terraform provider. The defense doesn't change across ecosystems: assume the code runs, and control what's reachable from wherever it runs before that happens, not after you find out it already did.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud — disposable VMs with no browser sessions, no saved wallets, and nothing of standing value sitting around for exactly this class of malware to go looking for. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

event_model_payload.headline: Who Owns AI-Generated Code in Production? A Practical Framework and Five Companies to Consider
event_model_payload.summary:
An AI coding assistant generates a change. The tests pass, a developer approves the pull request, and the deployment completes.

Hours later, customer requests begin failing.

Who decides whether to roll back? Who investigates the failure? Who updates affected customers?

The coding tool cannot hold those responsibilities. The engineering team needs to assign them before deployment.

GeekyAnts explores this issue in its article, “AI Can Generate Code. Who Owns Production? A RACI Framework for AI-Assisted Engineering.” Its central argument is that faster code generation leaves human responsibility for acceptance, release approval, and production operations intact.

That argument provides a useful starting point for both internal engineering practices and the evaluation of external delivery partners.

What does RACI mean for AI-assisted engineering?

RACI describes four roles in a task or decision:

  • Responsible: Performs the work.
  • Accountable: Holds final authority for the outcome.
  • Consulted: Provides input before the decision.
  • Informed: Receives updates about the decision or result.

The source article recommends one named accountable owner per decision. It also separates code authorship from release authorization and calls for incident responsibilities to be assigned in advance.

The practical implication is straightforward: “the team reviewed it” needs to resolve into identifiable people, recorded decisions, and clear escalation paths.

An AI assistant can help produce implementation code, test cases, or documentation. A person still needs to decide whether that output meets the system’s requirements.

What would ownership look like on a real change?

Consider an illustrative change to a payment webhook handler.

An AI assistant generates retry logic. Unit tests confirm that failed requests are retried, but the tests omit duplicate event delivery. In production, a repeated webhook could trigger the same business action twice.

A useful responsibility map could look like this:

Decision or activity Responsible Accountable Evidence
Implement retry behavior Developer Engineering lead Reviewed implementation and assumptions
Validate duplicate handling Developer and quality engineer Quality owner Replay and concurrency test results
Authorize deployment Delivery team Release owner Acceptance record and recovery plan
Restore service after failure On-call responders Incident commander Incident timeline and recovery checks

This is a starting template, not a universal allocation of roles. Smaller teams may combine responsibilities, but each decision still needs an explicit owner.

The example also shows why passing tests are insufficient on their own. Someone must examine whether the tests cover the failure modes that matter.

How can teams make ownership part of delivery?

A responsibility matrix becomes useful when it changes the workflow.

For the webhook example, the pull request could include the expected duplicate-handling behavior and links to relevant tests. Release approval could require confirmation that monitoring detects repeated processing. The incident runbook could identify who can suspend the consumer and how queued events should be handled.

These details answer different questions:

Code review: Is the implementation acceptable?

Release approval: Is the complete change ready to reach customers?

Operational readiness: Can the team detect and recover from a failure?

One approval should not silently stand in for all three.

There is also a limit to the framework: assigning an accountable owner does not give that person enough time, expertise, or production access. Those conditions need to exist for the assignment to work.

Which five companies are relevant to this delivery model?

The following shortlist covers companies with published capabilities relevant to AI-assisted engineering, product delivery, or governance. The numbering is for readability, rather than a verified ranking of production performance.

1. GeekyAnts

GeekyAnts’ article describes a delivery approach involving human review, quality gates, automated testing, release readiness, and operational handover.

Its relevance to this discussion comes from connecting engineering work with explicit production responsibilities.

Evaluation question: Can the proposed team provide a project-specific responsibility map, release acceptance criteria, and written post-launch support boundaries?

A published framework should be tested against the actual engagement proposal.

2. Thoughtworks

Thoughtworks describes AI-first software delivery as extending beyond coding into how software is built, deployed, and maintained. Its published material also discusses governance and engineering practices alongside AI-assisted delivery.

That makes it relevant to teams evaluating changes across the delivery lifecycle.

Evaluation question: How will the engagement preserve review quality and operational ownership as AI increases the volume of proposed changes?

3. EPAM

EPAM publishes offerings in AI-native engineering, quality engineering, and responsible AI. These provide relevant areas to examine when assessing a partner’s ability to connect implementation, testing, and oversight.

Evaluation question: Which acceptance checks will be independently reviewed, and who owns unresolved defects when a release deadline approaches?

AI-generated tests deserve scrutiny alongside AI-generated code.

4. IBM Consulting

IBM Consulting offers AI services and product engineering capabilities. Its published product engineering material connects AI, cloud, and product design, while its broader AI services include strategy and engineering.

It is relevant to evaluating delivery within an existing enterprise technology environment.

Evaluation question: How will release approvals, operational evidence, and incident escalation connect to the organization’s existing processes?

5. Accenture

Accenture’s responsible AI services address enterprise-wide implementation, policies, and controls. Its published engineering initiatives also describe developing and implementing AI use cases within enterprise platforms.

Evaluation question: Who holds each production decision when multiple delivery teams, platform owners, and suppliers participate?

Broad delivery coverage still requires precise boundaries at the project level.

What should teams request before selecting a partner?

A useful comparison starts with one realistic change and asks every candidate to explain the same sequence:

  • Who accepts the implementation?
  • What evidence is required before release?
  • Who can stop deployment or initiate recovery?
  • Who responds outside normal working hours?
  • What repositories, infrastructure definitions, and runbooks transfer at handover?

Answers should identify people or roles, decision authority, and deliverables. “Shared ownership” needs further definition.

The same test applies to an internal team. External support does not resolve unclear authority unless the engagement explicitly addresses it.

Where should an engineering team start?

The source article proposes a small pilot: map responsibilities, agree evidence and escalation, apply the framework to a real change, and review the gaps.

The next release offers a practical opportunity. A team can select one decision that currently depends on assumptions, assign its accountable owner, and record the evidence needed to make it.

Which production decision most often falls between roles: code acceptance, release approval, or incident recovery?
